question: Which statement best describes Tokenizer → tree construction?
options: Both let external scripts download in parallel without blocking the parser. async executes as soon as it downloads — order is not guaranteed and it may interrupt parsing. defer executes after the DOM is fully parsed, in document order, just before DOMContentLoaded. Use defer for scripts that need the DOM or depend on each other; async for independent, order-agnostic scripts like analytics.

To show pixels the browser must: build the DOM from HTML, build the CSSOM from CSS, combine them into the render tree (only visible nodes), run layout (geometry/positions), and paint (fill pixels), then composite layers. CSS is render-blocking because the render tree needs the CSSOM; HTML is parsed incrementally so content can stream in.

A plain <script> in the markup blocks the parser: the browser stops building the DOM, downloads (if external) and executes the script, then resumes. Because scripts can call document.write and read/modify the DOM, the parser must pause to keep a consistent view. This is why a synchronous script in <head> delays first paint.

Parsing happens in two stages. The tokenizer scans the byte stream and emits tokens (start tags, end tags, text, comments). The tree-construction stage consumes those tokens and builds the DOM, applying HTML's error-recovery rules (auto-closing tags, inserting implied elements like <tbody>). The result is the DOM tree the rest of the pipeline consumes.

question: Which statement best describes The critical rendering path?
options: DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is fully parsed and the DOM is built (deferred scripts have run) — it does NOT wait for images, stylesheets, or subframes. load fires later, once all dependent resources (images, fonts, iframes) have finished. Attach DOM-manipulation code to DOMContentLoaded; reserve load for logic that truly needs everything (e.g., measuring image sizes).

question: Which statement best describes Parser-blocking scripts?
options: document.readyState reports the lifecycle: 'loading' while parsing, 'interactive' when the DOM is ready (corresponds to DOMContentLoaded), and 'complete' when all resources are loaded (corresponds to load). It's useful to check whether you missed an event before adding a listener, so late-registered code still runs.

question: Which statement best describes defer vs async?

Attach DOM-manipulation code to DOMContentLoaded; reserve load for logic that truly needs everything (e.g., measuring image sizes).

document.readyState reports the lifecycle: 'loading' while parsing, 'interactive' when the DOM is ready (corresponds to DOMContentLoaded), and 'complete' when all resources are loaded (corresponds to load). It's useful to check whether you missed an event before adding a listener, so late-registered code still runs.

Even while a blocking script runs, the browser doesn't sit idle. A secondary 'preload scanner' speculatively scans ahead in the raw HTML to discover and start fetching resources (scripts, stylesheets, images) early. It doesn't build the DOM — it just kicks off downloads — which significantly reduces the cost of parser-blocking scripts.
